14959               	;
14960               	; #if NES
14961               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14962               	; 	' THE ATTRIBUTE TABLE -- the NES's only way of giving two parts of the
14963               	; 	' screen different colours.
14964               	; 	'
14965               	; 	' 64 bytes at $23C0. Each byte covers FOUR character rows and four
14966               	; 	' columns, split into four 2x2 quadrants of two bits each: bits 0-1 top
14967               	; 	' left, 2-3 top right, 4-5 bottom left, 6-7 bottom right.
14968               	; 	'
14969               	; 	' The picture sits three rows down for overscan, which lands the regions
14970               	; 	' on block boundaries almost by luck:
14971               	; 	'
14972               	; 	'   byte row 0   name rows 0-3    the HUD is row 3  -> bottom quads P1
14973               	; 	'   byte row 1   name rows 4-7    the sky, top half -> P2, bottom -> P3
14974               	; 	'   byte rows 2+ name rows 8-29   the store         -> P0
14975               	; 	'
14976               	; 	' $50 is "bottom two quadrants on palette 1"; $FA is "top two on palette
14977               	; 	' 2, bottom two on palette 3", which is what splits the sunset into a
14978               	; 	' blue band over a warm one. Written as bare literals because this is the
14979               	; 	' one place the bit layout is visible, and naming them would hide it.
14980               	; 	'
14981               	; 	' 64 VPOKEs is 192 bytes of PPU queue, and WRTVRM waits when the 64-byte
14982               	; 	' buffer fills, so this paces itself across three frames and cannot
14983               	; 	' overrun vblank the way a single big SCREEN blit can.
14984               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES WHITE ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
14985               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
14986               	; 	'
14987               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
14988               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14989               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14990               	; 	' palette, dark blue and white, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14991               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14992               	; 	'
14993               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14994               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14995               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14996               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
14997               	; 	'
14998               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
14999               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
15000               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
15001               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
15002               	; 	' these beside it.
15003               	; 	'
15004               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
15005               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
15006               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
15007               	; nes_boxatt:
15008               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 3
15009               	; 		VPOKE #nav,85
15010               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
15011               	; 	NEXT nai
15012               	; 	RETURN
15013               	;
15014               	; nes_attr:
15015               	; 	#nav = 9152			' $23C0
15016               	; 	' $55, NOT $50 -- ALL FOUR QUADRANTS ON P1, not just the bottom two.
15017               	; 	'
15018               	; 	' $50 put the HUD's own row (name row 2) on P1 and left rows 0-1 on P0.
15019               	; 	' That was invisible while text sat on the backdrop, and stopped being so
15020               	; 	' the moment the font gained a PAPER: rows 0-1 are blank cells, and a blank
15021               	; 	' cell is all paper, so they came out in P0's index 1 -- the store's GREEN
15022               	; 	' -- as a green band above the score line. Nothing is drawn up there, so
15023               	; 	' putting the whole byte on P1 costs nothing and the HUD reads as one band
15024               	; 	' of dark blue running into the sky.
15025               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
15026               	; 		VPOKE #nav,85
15027               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
15028               	; 	NEXT nai
15029               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
15030               	; 		VPOKE #nav,170			' $AA -- the whole sky band on P2, no second palette
15031               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
15032               	; 	NEXT nai
15033               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 47
15034               	; 		VPOKE #nav,0
15035               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
15036               	; 	NEXT nai
15037               	; 	RETURN
15038               	; #endif
15039               	;

15041               	; 	' DIV on this CPU, and only run when the value actually changes.

15499               	;
15500               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15501               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15502               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15503               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15504               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15505               	; 	'
15506               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15507               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15508               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15509               	; 	'
15510               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15511               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15512               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15513               	; 	'
15514               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15515               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15516               	; 	'
15517               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15518               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15519               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15520               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15521               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15522               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15523               	; 	'
15524               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15525               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15526               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15527               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15528               	; 	'
15529               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15530               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15531               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15532               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)

15649               	;
15650               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15651               	; 	'
15652               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15653               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15654               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15655               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15656               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15657               	; 	'
15658               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15659               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15660               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15661               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15662               	; 	' counting stops.
15663               	;
15664               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15665               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15666               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15667               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15668               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15669               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15670               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15671               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15672               	; 	'
15673               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15674               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15675               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
15676               	;

16028               	;
16029               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
16030               	; 	'
16031               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
16032               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
16033               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
16034               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
16035               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
16036               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
16037               	; 	'
16038               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
16039               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
16040               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
16041               	; 	'
16042               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
16043               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
16044               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
16045               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
16046               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
16047               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
16048               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
16049               	; 	'
16050               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
16051               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
16052               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
16053               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
16054               	; 	'
16055               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
16056               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
16057               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
16058               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
16059               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
16060               	; 	'
16061               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
16062               	; 	' did not finish.
16063               	; pause_beat:
16064               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT
16065               	; 	GOSUB snd_pend
16066 FA46 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     FA48 A980     
16067 FA4A FA1E     	data cvb_SND_PEND
16068               	; 	' TWICE AS LONG AS IT WAS, AND IN ONE PLACE. The reason box waits one beat
16069               	; 	' and GAME OVER two, so doubling the beat doubles both and keeps them in
16070               	; 	' proportion -- where adding a third and a fourth `GOSUB pause_beat` at the
16071               	; 	' call sites would have cost code to say the same thing worse.
16072               	; 	'
16073               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNT AND NOT THE WAITS. sfx_tick runs once per pass, so it

16446               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16447               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16448               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16449               	; 	'
16450               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16451               	; 	'
16452               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16453               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16454               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16455               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16456               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16457               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16458               	; 	'
16459               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16460               	; 	'
16461               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16462               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16463               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16464               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16465               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16466               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16467               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16468               	; 	'
16469               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16470               	; 	'
16471               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16472               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16473               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16474               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16475               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16476               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16477               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16478               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16479               	; 	'
16480               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16481               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16482               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16483               	; 	'
16484               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16485               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16486               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16487               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16488               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16489               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16490               	; 	'
16491               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16492               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16493               	; 	'
16494               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16495               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16496               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16497               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16498               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16499               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16500               	; 	'
16501               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16502               	; 	'
16503               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16504               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16505               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
16506               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
16507               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
16508               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not
16509               	; 	' back to 7.

16708               	;
16709               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16710               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16711               	; 	'
16712               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16713               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16714               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16715               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16716               	; 	'
16717               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16718               	; 	'
16719               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16720               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16721               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16722               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16723               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16724               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16725               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16726               	; 	'
16727               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16728               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16729               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16730               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16731               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16732               	; 	'
16733               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16734               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16735               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16736               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16737               	; 	#if TI994A
16738               	; 	BANK 2
16739      013E     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$

16877               	;
16878               	; 	' THE COLOUR TABLE, 472 bytes of the same value ($B4 = black ink on dark blue).
16879               	; 	'
16880               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col, which is ONE synchronous call that
16881               	; 	' writes all three screen thirds (define_color always does the LDIRVM3 triple
16882               	; 	' copy). It replaced a VPOKE loop that wrote this one value 1,416 times paced by
16883               	; 	' 24 WAITs -- the largest scripted delay in the boot, and the reason the title
16884               	; 	' screen used to fill in visibly rather than appearing at once.
16885               	; 	'
16886               	; 	' EIGHT BYTES PER CHARACTER, not one. Supply fewer and DEFINE COLOR reads
16887               	; 	' whatever follows in ROM as colour data, with no error at build or run time.

17213               	; 	' AND THE TITLE'S DISPLAY LIST, for the same reason as the font: walked
17214               	; 	' once by title_draw, at boot and on a return to the title, and never
17215               	; 	' during play. title_draw selects bank 2 around its walk.
17216               	; 	'
17217               	; 	' ITS MESSAGE BOXES DID NOT COME WITH IT. They are the same format and
17218               	; 	' were in the same generated file, which is what made this worth doing
17219               	; 	' carefully: they are walked when a ROUND ENDS, mid-game, so on bank 2
17220               	; 	' they would have returned bytes from the wrong page at the moment a life
17221               	; 	' is lost -- and with no error at build or run time. gentitle.py now
17222               	; 	' writes them to title.bas below, which stays in bank 1.
17223               	; 	INCLUDE "titledl.bas"
17224               	; 	' ==================================================
17225               	; 	' THE TITLE SCREEN, AS A DISPLAY LIST
17226               	; 	' Generated by assets/gentitle.py -- do not edit here.
17227               	; 	'
17228               	; 	' row, col, length, then `length` bytes; 255 ends.
17229               	; 	' Walked by title_draw only.
17230               	; 	'
17231               	; 	' LIVES IN BANK 2, with the fonts, because it is read ONCE
17232               	; 	' -- at boot and on a return to the title. title_draw
17233               	; 	' selects bank 2 around its walk and restores bank 1.
17234               	; 	' The message boxes in title.bas are the same format and
17235               	; 	' CANNOT come with it: they are read when a round ends.
17236               	; 	' ==================================================
17237               	;

17449               	; 	INCLUDE "art.bas"
17450               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
17451               	; 	'
17452               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
17453               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
17454               	; 	' being small sprites.
17455               	; 	'
17456               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
17457               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
17458               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
17459               	; 	'
17460               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
17461               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
17462               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
17463               	;
17464               	; spr_kelly:	' Kelly: RIGHT hat/face/two merged run bodies/two FREE slots/duck hat/face/body, then the same LEFT (+36). The run bodies carry tunic AND legs, so a frame is one sprite, and standing is run frame 1. Patterns 0..68
17465               cvb_SPR_KELLY

18705               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
18706               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
18707               	; 	'
18708               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
18709               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
18710               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
18711               	; 	'
18712               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
18713               	; 	' blit is
18714               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
18715               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
18716               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
18717               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
18718               	; 	'
18719               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
18720               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
18721               	; 	'
18722               	; 	' template ids:
18723               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
18724               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
18725               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
18726               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
18727               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
18728               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
18729               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
18730               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2
18731               	; 	'   8 T_ROOF3
18732               	; 	'   9 T_ROOF4
18733               	; 	'   10 T_ROOF5
18734               	; 	'   11 T_ROOF6
18735               	; 	'   12 T_ROOF7
18736               	; 	'   13 T_END_W
18737               	; 	'   14 T_END_E
18738               	;
18739               	; stor_tpl:	' 15 templates x 160 bytes
18740               cvb_STOR_TPL

19355               	;
19356               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
19357               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
19358               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
19359               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
19360               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
19361               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
19362               	; #if NES
19363               	; nes_sky2c:
19364               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
19365               	; nes_bldlc:
19366               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
19367               	; #endif
19368               	;
19369               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
19370               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
19371               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
19372               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
19373               	; 	'
19374               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
19375               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
19376               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
19377               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).
